d: One of eight WW2 deep-level shelters — 1,200 ft of tunnels under the common; later housed Windrush arrivals. The drum-shaped entrance still stands.
WW2 deep-level shelter — its white entrance rotunda sits right on the common by the tube station.
WW2 deep-level shelter; the only one whose tunnels are still largely untouched. Entrance drum on Bedford Road.
WW2 deep-level shelter — the entrance drum is now the famous war-memorial mural roundabout.
WW2 deep-level shelter under Camden's platforms; its Buck Street drum hides behind the market.
WW2 deep-level shelter on Downside Crescent — 8,000 bunks; later a secure archive store.
The Eisenhower Centre — WW2 deep shelter that served as General Eisenhower's London signals base.
Became the Kingsway telephone exchange — a Cold War hardened exchange with its own artesian well and bar.
The Piccadilly's Strand branch, closed 1994 — sheltered the Elgin Marbles in WW2, now London's favourite film set.
Closed 1932; Churchill's secret Railway Executive bunker in the Blitz. The ox-blood facade hides in a Mayfair side street.
Closed 1934 — its lift shafts ran WW2 anti-aircraft control for London. Facade survives on Cottage Place.
Central line stop closed 1933 when Holborn opened a block away; the surface building is gone but the platforms remain.
Piccadilly line, closed 1932 — the ox-blood Leslie Green building still stands whole near King's Cross.
Closed 1924; now a shop and an escape-room in the old lift shafts. Subject of a John Betjeman ghost story.
Northern line, closed 1922 — its ventilation tower still pokes up beside the road.
The 1890 City & South London Railway's original terminus — abandoned after just ten years; tunnels used as air-raid shelters.
Fake five-storey house facades hiding an open cutting where Circle line trains vented steam — knock and nobody answers.
London's tram subway under Kingsway, closed 1952 — the northern portal ramp still dives under Southampton Row.
The Post Office's own driverless tube (1927–2003), 6.5 miles under the streets — ride a bit of it at the Postal Museum.
Brunel's 1843 tunnel — the first under any navigable river — now carries the Windrush line. The engine house is a museum.
A vaulted Byzantine-style pedestrian subway under Crystal Palace Parade, built for the vanished High Level station.
Intact platforms on the Parkland Walk — and the spriggan sculpture climbing from a wall that inspired a Stephen King story.
Abandoned surface platforms above the tube station, left from the unfinished Northern Heights plan — now a bat sanctuary.
The Metropolitan's vast depot — largest on the Underground, with its own social club and history stretching to 1882.
Stabling for the Northern line at the end of the world's (once) longest railway tunnel — 17 miles from East Finchley.
Piccadilly line depot — watch the trains fan out from the Northfields platforms.
Engineering depot since 1872, hidden behind West Kensington — where Underground track machines sleep.
Central line's western depot — built for the 1948 extension, with a fleet of heritage engineering stock.
Remains of the 1908 Franco-British Exhibition station — bits of platform still visible from passing Central line trains.
A tunnelling shield of the Greathead type abandoned in place — glimpsed from the platform ends in the old City & South London tunnels.
